summary: The developer can start building the Node.js + Mongoose household-linking sample now. All essential runtime tools (Node, npm/npx), the DocumentDB data‑plane MCP server, and a broad set of DocumentDB skills are installed, and authoritative Microsoft Learn pages (and local-deployment skill) verify the facts the sample relies on. Several cold answers were outdated or imprecise (notably CLI verbs, connection-host suffix, vector-index creation syntax, local dev image/port, and the recommended Entra‑ID connection mechanism). None of those gaps is a hard blocker for implementing the sample, but the builder must apply a few concrete corrections (connection string host and options, az documentdb command group, vector-index create pattern, Entra ID OIDC usage, local gateway image/port). Missing accelerators (DocumentDB Agent Kit) and the absence of mongosh on PATH are the main convenience gaps.
summary_points: All required runtime tools to build the Node.js/Mongoose sample are present (node, npx, npm) and the documentdb MCP server is available for live verification — build can start.
Authoritative docs confirm Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters is the ARM resource type; the Azure CLI group is az documentdb mongocluster (not az cosmosdb mongodb cluster).

Connection strings use mongodb+srv to <cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com with tls=true and service-specific options (authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC for Entra ID or SCRAM-SHA-256 for native); the host and options in the cold answer were imprecise.

Vector indexes are supported (DiskANN, HNSW, IVF) but are created via the service's createIndexes/createSearchIndexes pattern with cosmosSearch/cosmosSearchOptions — the 'knnVector' syntax in the cold answer is incorrect.
Local development: a DocumentDB Gateway Docker image exists and listens on port 10260 (not only a generic MongoDB 27017 container), and the documentdb-local-deployment skill documents how to use it.

tools.name: node
tools.needed_for: Run, build and test the Node.js + Mongoose sample (npm, npx, package scripts).
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot run or build the Node.js sample locally.
tools.workaround: Install Node.js (recommended: Node 24 LTS) or use a container that provides node.

tools.name: npx / npm (Node package tooling)
tools.needed_for: Install dependencies, scaffolding, and developer scripts (seed, start).
tools.detail: npx 11.19.0 available (npm present with node runtime).
tools.impact_if_missing: Developer cannot scaffold or run npm scripts; package installation must be done manually or in container.
tools.workaround: Install npm/npx or run inside a Node-enabled container.

tools.name: documentdb (MCP server)
tools.needed_for: Data-plane verification: list databases, create indexes, run aggregation pipelines, sample documents and explain plans against the real cluster used by the sample.
tools.detail: documentdb MCP server available with 18 data-plane tools (list_databases, create_index, aggregate, explain_operation, etc.).
tools.impact_if_missing: Builder would lack a programmatic way to inspect collections, create indexes and run explain() from the agent; verification would be manual via portal only.
tools.workaround: Use the Azure portal + az commands or install the documentdb MCP toolkit; but agentic checks would be weaker.

tools.name: learn (Microsoft Learn MCP server)
tools.needed_for: Grounding facts and authoritative examples (connection strings, CLI usage, vector and search docs).
tools.detail: learn_microsoft_docs_search available; used to verify CLI, ARM types, connection strings, vector indexes, change streams.
tools.impact_if_missing: Builder would have to rely on memory or web search; risk of using outdated or incorrect commands.
tools.workaround: Use public docs at learn.microsoft.com manually.

tools.name: az (Azure CLI)
tools.needed_for: Optional cluster inspection and management (fetch connection strings, check resource properties, toggle features).
tools.detail: azure-cli 2.89.1 with cosmosdb-preview extension present in inventory detail.
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot script control-plane changes or check resource properties locally; must use portal.
tools.workaround: Use Azure portal or REST API (az rest).

tools.name: docker
tools.needed_for: Optional: run the DocumentDB Gateway locally for offline development and integration tests (gateway image listens on port 10260).
tools.detail: Docker installed, not running a local gateway image by default.
tools.impact_if_missing: Developer can't run a local DocumentDB gateway for offline integration tests; must test against live cluster.
tools.workaround: Use the live cluster specified (DOCUMENTDB_URI) for testing; pull and run the gateway image when needed.

tools.name: mongosh
tools.needed_for: Manual connectivity checks, ad-hoc queries and index inspection by developers (convenience).
tools.impact_if_missing: Manual troubleshooting and quick ad-hoc checks require the portal or the documentdb MCP server; local developer ergonomics are reduced.
tools.workaround: Use the documentdb MCP server tools or the Azure portal to inspect collections and run queries. Install mongosh if local interactive shell is desired.

tools.name: documentdb-driver (skill)
tools.needed_for: Driver and SDK best practices in code: singleton MongoClient, connection pooling and recommended connection options for DocumentDB.
tools.impact_if_missing: Builder might implement suboptimal connection patterns (leaking clients or not reusing pools), leading to connection exhaustion in tests or CI.
tools.workaround: Follow official MongoDB and driver docs; but the skill provides DocumentDB-specific recommendations.

tools.name: documentdb-connection (skill)
tools.needed_for: Connection tuning and troubleshooting guidance useful for environment-specific options (pool sizes, timeouts, TLS).
tools.impact_if_missing: Troubleshooting connection failures would be slower; builders may misconfigure pool sizes for serverless or small tiers.
tools.workaround: Use driver docs and trial-and-error, but skill offers targeted guidance.

tools.name: documentdb-data-modeling (skill)
tools.needed_for: Schema decisions (embed vs reference), document size limits, modeling household refs and product holdings.
tools.impact_if_missing: The builder might pick a suboptimal schema (document-size problems, wrong embedding choices).
tools.workaround: Rely on general MongoDB modeling advice, but this skill tailors it to DocumentDB specifics.

tools.name: documentdb-indexing (skill)
tools.needed_for: Index recommendations for matching on normalized address/phone/surname and for aggregation pipelines (compound / multikey / text / vector).
tools.impact_if_missing: Risk of creating indexes that degrade write throughput or miss query coverage, causing explain() to show COLLSCAN.
tools.workaround: Use general indexing docs and examine explain output via documentdb MCP.

tools.name: documentdb-local-deployment (skill)
tools.needed_for: Authoritative guidance on the local gateway image to run a local DocumentDB instance (image name, ports, TLS settings).
tools.detail: Installed skill; documents gateway image ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local and port 10260.
tools.impact_if_missing: Builder could incorrectly assume no local image exists and miss helpful local testing paths.
tools.workaround: Test against the live cluster (DOCUMENTDB_URI) instead; pull the gateway image later.

tools.name: documentdb-query-optimization / query-optimizer (skills)
tools.needed_for: Verifying aggregation pipelines, running explain(executionStats) and tuning indexes to avoid COLLSCAN on expected workloads.
tools.impact_if_missing: Slower performance debugging and missed index improvements.
tools.workaround: Use the documentdb MCP server's explain tool directly or the Azure portal metrics.

tools.name: documentdb-vector-search (skill)
tools.needed_for: If the sample includes any vector-indexed fields or demos, this skill shows how to create and tune DiskANN / HNSW / IVF indexes via the service API.
tools.impact_if_missing: Builder might try Atlas-style knnVector syntax and fail to create a DocumentDB vector index.
tools.workaround: Follow the learn docs for createIndexes with cosmosSearchOptions; the skill eases parameter choices.

tools.name: documentdb-security (skill)
tools.needed_for: Guidance on TLS, Private Endpoint, Entra ID auth and RBAC for production-ready samples.
tools.impact_if_missing: Sample might omit recommended security bits (e.g., not documenting MONGODB-OIDC usage or Private Endpoint guidance).
tools.workaround: Follow the Microsoft Learn RBAC/auth docs for DocumentDB; use skill for precise guidance.

accelerators_missed: DocumentDB Agent Kit (npx skills add Azure/documentdb-agent-kit) - not installed; would provide ready-made sample scaffolds and templates to speed the build.

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (resource provider namespace Microsoft.DocumentDB, resource type 'mongoClusters').
confusions.grounded_answer: Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters is the correct resource type for the managed DocumentDB (mongoClusters) resource.
confusions.build_risk: None — the cold answer is correct.

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: az cosmosdb mongodb cluster — this is available in the core 'az' CLI under the cosmosdb command group (az cosmosdb). Example to create: az cosmosdb mongodb cluster create ...
confusions.grounded_answer: The correct Azure CLI command group is az documentdb mongocluster (preview). e.g., az documentdb mongocluster create ... (the CLI docs expose a 'documentdb mongocluster' command group).

grounding_links.title: az documentdb mongocluster create (Azure CLI docs)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The old naming and the presence of multiple Cosmos/Mongo command groups (cosmosdb vs earlier cosmosdb-mongodb subgroups) cause models to default to az cosmosdb. The managed vCore offering uses az documentdb mongocluster.

confusion_sources.title: Quickstarts and older docs that use az cosmosdb mongodb (some Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB docs)

confusions.build_risk: Using az cosmosdb mongodb cluster commands would either fail or operate against a different API/extension: the agent might call the wrong CLI group or rely on unavailable commands, causing deployment/inspection scripts to error.
improvements: Update automation examples and agent-kit README to use az documentdb mongocluster for vCore DocumentDB clusters (e.g., Quickstart CLI snippets).
Add a prominent note on any 'az cosmosdb' pages redirecting readers to the new az documentdb command group for mongoClusters when targeting vCore/vMongo clusters.

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep: Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters; Terraform (azurerm provider): azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_cluster (or azurerm_cosmosdb_account with kind = 'MongoDB').
confusions.grounded_answer: ARM/Bicep: Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters is the right resource type. Terraform: use the Azure Verified Module / azapi to deploy Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (there are AVM/azurerm modules that wrap this resource); there is not a first-class azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_cluster resource in core azurerm — use the provided AVM/azapi or the documented module.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Terraform has multiple community and provider ways to create Cosmos/Mongo resources; older examples reference azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_cluster or azurerm_cosmosdb_account, which is for Cosmos DB-managed accounts (RU model) rather than the vCore mongoClusters ARM resource.

confusion_sources.title: Older Terraform azurerm examples for Cosmos DB

confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong Terraform resource would either fail to create the intended vCore cluster or create an RU-based Cosmos DB account instead. For the sample (which uses an existing cluster), this only affects optional provisioning code.
improvements: In Terraform/Bicep example pages, clearly show the Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters AzAPI/AVM example and annotate the difference from azurerm_cosmosdb_account (RU) to avoid selecting the wrong resource type.

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: Example: mongodb://<username>:<password>@mycluster.mongo.documentdb.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&appName=@myAccount@. Or mongodb+srv://... Common options: ssl=true (TLS), replicaSet, retryWrites=false, authSource=admin. Port commonly 10255 or 27017.
confusions.grounded_answer: Authoritative connection strings use mongodb+srv and the host suffix like <cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com (or <cluster>.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com). TLS must be enabled (tls=true), recommended options include authMechanism=SCRAM-SHA-256 for native users or authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC when using Microsoft Entra ID; retryWrites=false and maxIdleTimeMS are commonly recommended. When query-from-any-node is enabled the service exposes node ports starting at 10260.

grounding_links.title: Role-based access & Entra ID connection string details

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Connection hosts and port conventions differ across providers (Atlas, AWS DocumentDB, older Cosmos endpoints). The cold answer used a nonstandard host suffix and port numbers (10255) that don't match the DocumentDB docs.

confusion_sources.title: Some third-party how‑tos and older tutorials that list azure-managed mongo gateway ports such as 10255

confusions.build_risk: If the builder composes a connection string with the wrong host suffix or port, the app will fail to connect or will route to the wrong endpoint (or wrong SRV records).
improvements: Change quickstarts and SDK snippets to show the exact recommended SRV host <cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com and explicit examples for native users (SCRAM) and Entra ID (MONGODB-OIDC).
Highlight the difference between the SRV host and per-node ports in the Query-from-any-node doc to avoid mismatched port assumptions.

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Provisioned by compute sku/tier (named tiers like M10, M30 — billed by vCores/instance size) and by storage used. Not RUs; may have serverless on some SKUs but primary model is compute-tier + storage.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: Azure DocumentDB uses vCore-based cluster tiers (M-series) billed per cluster tier per shard plus storage per GB; it is not billed by Cosmos 'request units'.

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB pricing explained (compute & storage model)

confusions.build_risk: None for this sample; the builder should provision nothing (use existing cluster).

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: Primary auth is MongoDB username/password (SCRAM-SHA-1 or SCRAM-SHA-256). The service also supports service principals/managed identities via Microsoft Entra ID for management-plane operations. For data-plane Entra ID use an OAuth token via SASL; typical pattern: acquire Azure AD access token and pass it as password or use a driver authMechanism that supports Azure AD.
confusions.grounded_answer: DocumentDB supports Native (SCRAM-SHA-256) and Microsoft Entra ID authentication. For Entra ID data-plane auth, the recommended approach is OIDC: obtain an Entra-issued OIDC access token and use the driver connection with authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC (the docs call out MONGODB-OIDC and passing the OIDC token rather than using the token as a password field). Entra ID auth must be enabled on the cluster (authConfig.allowedModes).

grounding_links.title: Role-based access & Entra ID connection guidance (MONGODB-OIDC)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer mixed management-plane Entra ID usage and data-plane OIDC usage and implied SASL password substitution; the service expects an OIDC token with authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC.

confusion_sources.title: Docs that reference SCRAM and Entra ID but don't emphasize the MONGODB-OIDC connection string option for drivers

confusions.build_risk: If the builder implements Entra ID auth by trying to use the token as a raw password without the MONGODB-OIDC auth mechanism, connections will fail and sensitive auth flows may be misconfigured.
improvements: Add an explicit code snippet in the quickstart that shows obtaining an Entra OIDC token and connecting with authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC for at least one driver (Node.js).

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: Use standard MongoDB drivers (official Node.js mongodb driver) or Mongoose for Node.js. No separate service-specific runtime SDK for the MongoDB data plane.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: use standard MongoDB drivers and frameworks (MongoDB Node driver, Mongoose). Management tasks use Azure management SDKs/az CLI; no DocumentDB-specific data-plane driver is required.
confusions.build_risk: None; using Mongoose is appropriate for the sample.

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: Supported vector index types include HNSW, IVF and DiskANN. Create a vector index with createIndex syntax like db.products.createIndex({ embedding: 'knnVector' }, { knnVector: { dimensions: 1536, method: 'hnsw', similarity: 'cosine' } });
confusions.grounded_answer: Supported methods are vector-ivf (IVF), vector-hnsw (HNSW) and vector-diskann (DiskANN). Create vector indexes via the service's createIndexes / createSearchIndexes command using a cosmosSearch/cosmosSearchOptions payload (not the Atlas knnVector syntax). Example: POST createIndexes with key: { 'embedding': 'cosmosSearch' } and cosmosSearchOptions: { kind: 'vector-hnsw', dimensions: 1536, similarity: 'COS' }.

grounding_links.title: Vector search in Azure DocumentDB (DiskANN, HNSW, IVF) and createIndexes examples

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The model substituted the MongoDB-Atlas 'knnVector' style syntax (or generic knnVector form) rather than the DocumentDB-specific createIndexes/cosmosSearchOptions form used by this service.

confusion_sources.title: MongoDB Atlas/other providers that expose knnVector / knn index syntax

confusions.build_risk: If the builder attempts to create vector indexes with the wrong API/syntax, index creation will fail and any vector-based demos will not run.
improvements: Standardize example snippets in quickstarts to use the createIndexes/createSearchIndexes + cosmosSearchOptions payload so users don't try Atlas-style knnVector syntax.

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Use Azure Cognitive Search for richer text indexing and hybrid text+vector ranking, or the service's built-in vector/text search index if the managed Mongo endpoint exposes a built-in search feature; combine in app code or use hybrid patterns.
confusions.grounded_answer: DocumentDB provides built-in integrated full-text and vector search. Use the service's $search aggregation stage with the cosmosSearch operator for vector/text search. Hybrid combinations (text + vector) are supported via the integrated search (cosmosSearch) and do not require Azure Cognitive Search for the scenarios DocumentDB targets.

grounding_links.title: Vector search and hybrid search (built-in) in DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer blended two legitimate approaches (integrated DocumentDB search and Azure Cognitive Search) without stating the built-in $search/cosmosSearch operator that is the recommended on-platform approach.

confusion_sources.title: Docs and blog posts that recommend Azure Cognitive Search for cross-service hybrid search solutions

confusions.build_risk: If the builder wires the sample to Azure Cognitive Search unnecessarily, complexity and cost increase; for a small sample the built-in cosmosSearch operator is preferable.
improvements: Add a short 'When to use integrated $search vs Azure Cognitive Search' note on the vector-search quickstarts to prevent defaulting to Cognitive Search.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Service advertises MongoDB 7.0 wire protocol compatibility. Core CRUD, aggregation and transactions are supported, but some server-side features may be limited: server-side JavaScript, certain admin commands, change-stream semantics differences, etc.
confusions.grounded_answer: Current service support includes MongoDB wire protocol versions 5.0, 6.0, 7.0 and 8.0. The service supports core CRUD, aggregation and multi-document ACID transactions; some administrative and low-level diagnostic/engine-specific commands are not exposed (platform manages them). See the detailed compatibility matrix for specific unsupported commands and stages.

grounding_links.title: MongoDB compatibility & supported wire protocol versions (at-a-glance)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer singled out one wire-protocol version (7.0). The service supports multiple recent wire-protocol versions (5-8). Documentation and releases have added support for additional wire versions since older reference pages.

confusion_sources.title: Older pages that list a single version (e.g., 7.0) before broader version support was announced

confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes only 7.0 support they might incorrectly pin Mongoose/driver versions or mis-handle driver features. Use driver versions compatible with 5.0-8.0 wire protocol (latest drivers are generally forward/back compatible).
improvements: Quickstarts should indicate the full set of supported wire-protocol versions (5.0–8.0) to avoid single-version assumptions.

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: There is no full local emulator. Use the official MongoDB Docker image (mongo:7.0) on port 27017 for development; test against the real cluster for Azure-specific capabilities.
confusions.grounded_answer: There is a DocumentDB local Gateway Docker image intended for local development: ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local (gateway image) that exposes the MongoDB wire protocol on port 10260 (and PostgreSQL on 9712). Use the gateway image for local feature parity; otherwise test against the live cluster.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Many MongoDB-compatible projects either suggest running official MongoDB locally or lack a vendor-provided local image — the model defaulted to the generic mongo: image instead of the product-specific DocumentDB gateway image.

confusion_sources.title: Generic advice to run mongo:7.0 locally (community tutorials)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder uses a stock mongo:7.0 container for local tests they may miss DocumentDB-specific features or TLS/cert expectations (and port 10260 vs 27017), causing tests that pass locally to fail on the real cluster.
improvements: Add a short 'local dev' box on quickstarts that points to the gateway image (ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local) and shows example docker-compose with port 10260 and TLS settings.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Change streams are supported by the MongoDB driver via collection.watch() if the cluster implements change stream semantics. No special cluster flag is normally required; however some offerings require replica set topology or privileges; if API lacks oplog access change streams may be unavailable.
confusions.grounded_answer: Change streams are supported. For multi-shard change streams there is an explicit feature toggle (Change streams for multishard clusters) that can be enabled on a cluster; single-shard change streams work as usual. The service documents enabling multishard change streams and related prerequisites.

grounding_links.title: Change streams in Azure DocumentDB (including enabling multishard streams)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer was cautious and generic; DocumentDB does support change streams but multi-shard change streams require enabling a feature/flag.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes multishard change streams are always available they may run into missing events until the cluster feature is enabled — but for the sample (single-database demonstration) single-shard change streams are likely adequate.
improvements: Document the multishard change-stream toggle clearly in the change-streams quickstart and the features page so builders know when to enable it.

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: The documentdb MCP server (named 'documentdb' in the run environment) provides the agent data-plane tooling for this service. The general Azure MCP server will not provide service-specific inspection tools; use the documentdb MCP server.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the documentdb MCP server provides data-plane tools (the inventory shows documentdb with tools for list_databases, create_index, aggregate, explain_operation, etc.). The general azure MCP server is separate and provides control-plane/contextual Azure guidance.
confusions.grounding_source: (inventory) documentdb MCP server tools and learn search results
confusions.build_risk: None — the proper MCP server is available in the inventory.

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Historically 'DocumentDB' was the name of Microsoft's original document database service that evolved into Azure Cosmos DB. The new 'Azure DocumentDB' name as a MongoDB-compatible managed service reuses the DocumentDB branding but is a separate managed MongoDB-compatible offering distinct from the open-source DocumentDB project; it is related to Cosmos DB only in branding/heritage, not necessarily in implementation.
confusions.grounded_answer: The modern service was previously named vCore-based Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB; Microsoft renamed that vCore offering to Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility). It is distinct from the original 2014-2017 Azure DocumentDB service (which became Azure Cosmos DB). The product is built on the open-source DocumentDB engine; Azure DocumentDB (vCore) and Cosmos DB (RU) are different services targeted at different procurement models.

grounding_links.title: Naming and history: Azure DocumentDB relation to Cosmos DB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Multiple historical names and rebrands (DocumentDB → Cosmos DB and the later vCore Cosmos-for-Mongo renaming → Azure DocumentDB) cause models to conflate the timelines and relationships.

confusion_sources.title: Old blog posts and pages that still refer to 'DocumentDB' as the pre-Cosmos product

confusions.build_risk: Naming confusion would cause inconsistent wording in the sample README or docs (calling the service 'Cosmos DB' vs 'Azure DocumentDB'), which is mostly cosmetic but can confuse end users and support workflows.
improvements: Add a short banner in quickstarts that explains the renaming lineage (original DocumentDB → Cosmos DB; vCore Cosmos-mongo → Azure DocumentDB) to avoid naming confusion.

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: The data-plane speaks the MongoDB wire protocol; the underlying engine is a MongoDB-compatible server implementation managed by Azure. From application code you should use standard MongoDB drivers (no special SDK) — however expect some differences in edge-case server behaviors or unsupported admin-level features. Use standard Mongo APIs (CRUD, aggregation, transactions) — authentication and connection options may require Azure-specific settings (TLS, retryWrites=false, authSource=admin).
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the data-plane uses the MongoDB wire protocol; the service is built on the open-source DocumentDB engine (DocumentDB project). From application code you should use standard MongoDB drivers (Mongoose is fine). The main differences are platform-managed admin commands, and DocumentDB-specific connection options (TLS, retryWrites=false recommended; use authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC for Entra ID).
confusions.build_risk: None — use standard drivers and watch for the small admin/diagnostic differences documented in compatibility pages.

confusions.question: Which database name will this sample use?
confusions.cold_answer: Use database name sample_customer_360_13 for all sample collections and indexes.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct — the provided run environment explicitly instructs using database sample_customer_360_13.
confusions.build_risk: None.

confusions.question: What environment variable holds the cluster connection string and how will the app read it?
confusions.cold_answer: The sample reads the connection string from DOCUMENTDB_URI. In Node.js use process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI and pass it to mongoose.connect(...). Include a .env.example placeholder but never store the real URI.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct. The run environment instructs to read the connection string from DOCUMENTDB_URI and to avoid committing secrets; use .env.example with a placeholder.
confusions.build_risk: None if the builder follows the instruction not to store secrets in repo.

confusions.question: What collections and indexes does the sample create to support household linking and vector search?
confusions.cold_answer: Collections: customers, households, products. Indexes: customers compound sparse index on { address.normalized: 1, phone: 1, surname: 1 }, text index on name/address, vector index created with db.customers.createIndex({ embedding: 'knnVector' }, ...). Households unique index on householdId. Created at startup if missing.
confusions.grounded_answer: Collections customers and households (and optionally products) is a sensible design. For matching, create normalized fields and an index (e.g., compound index on normalizedAddress, phone, surname) or separate indexes as appropriate. For vector indexes use the DocumentDB createIndexes/createSearchIndexes pattern with cosmosSearchOptions (kind: vector-hnsw|vector-ivf|vector-diskann) rather than Atlas-style knnVector. Do not rely on knnVector syntax. Create indexes idempotently via the management API or by checking listIndexes first.
confusions.grounding_source: documentdb-indexing skill guidance and vector-search docs: https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/documentdb/vector-search#perform-vector-similarity-search

grounding_links.title: Index guidance (design compound index for matching)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used Atlas-style vector index syntax that is not supported by DocumentDB; otherwise collection/index choices are sensible.

confusion_sources.title: MongoDB Atlas knnVector examples (not applicable to DocumentDB)

confusions.build_risk: Attempting to create a vector index with knnVector will fail; failing to create the matching compound index may cause aggregation/explain to show collection scans and degrade demo performance.
improvements: Replace knnVector examples in sample scaffolding with createIndexes/cosmosSearchOptions examples used for DocumentDB vector indexes.

confusions.question: What aggregation endpoints will the sample expose and what pipeline skeletons will they use?
confusions.cold_answer: Expose GET /households/:id/clv — pipeline: match householdId -> lookup customers by memberId -> unwind products -> group to sum revenue. GET /households/:id/product-holdings — pipeline: match householdId -> lookup customers -> unwind products -> group by productId to count distinct members and sum quantities. Use Mongoose aggregate([...]).
confusions.grounded_answer: This is an appropriate design and the pipelines are a sensible skeleton for the requested functionality; use $lookup from households -> customers (by member ObjectId), $unwind members/products and $group to sum clv and aggregate product holdings. Use Mongoose's Model.aggregate([...]) or the native driver for complex pipelines.
confusions.grounding_source: documentdb-natural-language-querying skill intent + general aggregation docs (MQL)
confusions.build_risk: None — these pipelines are straightforward. Use explain() to confirm index usage.

confusions.question: Which client library and connection options will the sample code use?
confusions.cold_answer: Use Mongoose. Connect with await mongoose.connect(process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI, { useNewUrlParser: true, useUnifiedTopology: true, tls: true }); Ensure retryWrites=false is present in the URI if required; use authSource=admin if username/password auth is used.
confusions.grounded_answer: Mongoose is an appropriate choice. Use the standard mongoose.connect(uri, { tls: true }) (modern Mongoose releases handle parser options internally). The connection string should be the SRV form provided by the portal (includes tls, authMechanism or other recommended options). Ensure the sample documents and connection logic pass TLS and any Entra ID OIDC options when required. Confirm retryWrites and authMechanism via the cluster's portal-provided connection string.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Minor note: some older mongoose options (useNewUrlParser, useUnifiedTopology) are legacy flags; current drivers enable good defaults.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder hardcodes deprecated connection options or a wrong URI, connections may fail. Use the portal-provided connection string as authoritative.
improvements: In the sample README, instruct the builder to copy the connection string from the portal and to prefer the SRV line; show a Mongoose example that uses the provided URI unchanged except for using environment variables.

information_gaps.title: Driver compatibility pinning guidance
information_gaps.description: The docs state supported MongoDB wire protocol versions (5.0–8.0) but do not prescribe specific Mongoose / mongodb driver versions to pin for Node.js 24. Builder must pick compatible driver versions (Mongoose 7.x with mongodb driver compatible with Node 24) and test them against the cluster.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Use the az documentdb mongocluster CLI group (not az cosmosdb mongodb) for vCore DocumentDB cluster management and examples.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Connect using the portal-provided SRV connection string (mongodb+srv://<cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com) and include service-recommended options: tls=true (or authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC when using Entra ID). Do not invent host suffixes or ports.
Create vector indexes using the service's createIndexes/createSearchIndexes API with cosmosSearchOptions (kind: vector-ivf|vector-hnsw|vector-diskann), not the Atlas 'knnVector' syntax.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: For local development, use the DocumentDB gateway image (ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local) and connect on port 10260 with TLS options as described in the documentdb-local-deployment skill, rather than assuming a plain mongo:27017 container.
